_comment: What a FAILURE of each test costs a consumer. A passing test contributes
nothing; only failures score.
HOW A TEST GETS ITS CLASS. From what its failure means, per the glossary
below: a test that expects argus to block (a gate fires, a bad input is
rejected, a non-zero exit) fails OPEN when argus lets it through; a test
that expects argus to succeed fails CLOSED when argus errors out; a test of
something around the scan fails AUXILIARY. A test that can fail more than
one way reports which in its result ('class'), and that wins over the list
here -- N3 (exit 0 is open, exit 1 is closed) and N5 (a non-zero exit is
closed, a silent wrong-architecture pass is open) do. A test listed nowhere
is 'closed' by default.
WHAT IS CITED AND WHAT IS NOT. Be clear about this, because the two get
read as one thing:
CITED -- that a control which fails permissively is worse than one that
fails restrictively. Saltzer & Schroeder's fail-safe defaults [1] and
CWE-636 [2] are about exactly that, and they are why 'open' ranks above
'closed'. NIST SP 800-53A [3] is why each test is pass/fail rather than
scored: a control is satisfied or it is not.
NOT CITED -- the weights 10 / 3 / 1, and the third class. No source says
a silent pass is worth ten of a broken upload. They are a local judgement
about this suite, chosen so the ordering survives arithmetic, and they
should be argued with here rather than defended as literature.
A FOURTH CLASS WAS REMOVED. 'degraded' was added for argus's
ContainerScanResult.degraded -- a scan that ran with fewer sub-scanners than
were asked for. It had no members, no citation, a weight invented to sit
between two other invented weights, and a name a reader could not tell apart
from 'auxiliary'. Presenting it beside two genuinely-cited ideas implied a
taxonomy that does not exist. If a test is ever written whose failure means
'the scan silently covered less than was asked for', the honest home for it
is 'open': the defining feature is that nobody is told.
Labels are deliberately plain rather than 'fail-open'/'fail-closed'. That
vocabulary inverts across domains -- in physical security a fail-SAFE door
unlocks on power loss while a fail-SECURE one locks -- so a reader from a
safety-engineering background can read the jargon backwards.
Default is 'closed': a test that goes red without a declared class is
assumed to be argus breaking loudly, not argus lying.
_status_note: The word is the TEST OUTCOME, not a verdict on argus. A dashboard that
labels a product 'unsafe' on the strength of assertions its maintainers
have not agreed to is overstepping. The severity lives in the risk number,
the class counts and the sentence, all of which describe what was observed

glossary.open: argus reported success without actually running the check. Nothing warns you, so unscanned code can ship looking approved.
glossary.closed: argus stopped or errored when it should have worked. Your pipeline blocks, which is disruptive, but nothing slips past unnoticed.
glossary.auxiliary: Every requested scanner ran and the gate decided correctly, but something around the scan broke -- uploading the report, for instance. Security coverage is unchanged.

open.line: argus reports success without running the check it was asked for

closed.line: argus errors out where it should succeed -- the pipeline stops, nothing gets through

none.line: every defined test that ran, passed

auxiliary.line: an auxiliary path is broken; scans and gates still work

index.name: Risk index
index.caveat: The weights are a judgement call, not a measurement. The number adds up rather than averaging, so adding passing tests can never lower it. Only fixing a failure does.

references.ieee: MITRE, “CWE-636: Not failing securely (‘failing open’),” Common Weakness Enumeration. [Online].
references.note: failing open is a named weakness class, not a local preference

references.ieee: National Institute of Standards and Technology, “Assessing security and privacy controls in information systems and organizations,” NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5, Jan. 2022. [Online].
references.note: control assessment is binary — satisfied or other than satisfied — which is why each test is pass/fail rather than scored

_why_open: R6, C3-C6, D3, D4, E8, S13, S14 and S18 all assert that argus FAILS a run:
a severity gate firing, a build gate firing, missing registry credentials
being rejected, an SCN category threshold being enforced. If one of them
goes red, argus let through something it was asked to stop -- the
E5 and E9 are the same class observed directly: a scan naming no
recognised scanner, and a remote scan with an empty image_ref, both report
E6 and A5 assert that argus REJECTS an input -- a typo'd scanner name, two
containers with the same name. If one goes red, argus accepted it and
scanned less than it was asked to (the typo'd scanner, the container the
duplicate replaced) while reporting success. They were left at the 'closed'
default until an audit against the glossary.
